I'm not taking the bucket. The robot would notice. And he'd notice politely, which is the worst part.
A noticeboard with test results. Hundreds of sheets, all with grades and all with a column for cake. The cake column is empty.
Test subject 12: "Asked about the cake. Was reset." Test subject 33: "Did not ask about the cake. Was reset." Fair.
Yellow and black stripes on the floor. They say: caution. Caution of what, they don't say, and that's called design.
I stand on a yellow stripe. Nothing happens. Then on a black one. Nothing either. Pretty disappointing for so much warning.
A lamp on the ceiling, dripping next to it. Someone mopped here for years, and it's still dripping. That's called Sisyphus with a mop.
The drop lands right next to the bucket, every single time. I'm sure it does it on purpose.
A passage under the city. Neon behind me, concrete ahead. The city has a basement, and the basement has a door.
Something is humming somewhere at the back. Big and patient. Like a fridge that rules the world.
The robot's gone, but the floor is still wet. He meant it right to the end.
You can still see the last circle of mopping on the floor. A perfect circle, like a farewell letter.
He mops in circles. Always circles. If he ever mops a straight line, something's happened.
Tuna for a robot. He'd politely accept the tin and politely have no idea what to do with it.
Dog biscuits for a caretaker? He doesn't have a dog, he has a mop, and the mop doesn't eat.
And what are items one and two?
Nineteen years without oil. Let me see what I've got in my bag.
I'll be back. Really.
A robot who spent nineteen years on the second item because the first was too hard. I see myself in him.
In German, 08/15 means: standard. Nothing special. Run of the mill. People used to say it about things that did exactly what you expected.
He wears it on his chest. That's either very sad or very honest.
You just waved your hand and lied to a robot. I saw it.
I shall see it again, in my dreams, and I shall laugh every time.
He's still squeaking. And you've got oil in your bag.
He's happy. A robot was given a list and he's happy.
I have a list too, and I am not. Mine is missing tuna, and you can tell.
I said it while packing: for everything that squeaks, tin heads included.
Nobody listens to me, and yet I am always right. That is my cross, and I bear it with composure.
He's fed me into a world-domination AI. I'm going to be its loudspeaker.
I've been worse things, young man. I've already been wet several times today.
Water in a bucket, on the floor, drinkable.
That is the first civilised facility in this world, and of all things a robot set it up.
Test subject 47: "Very good, but asked for too little cake."
He mops in circles, and I walk in circles before I lie down.
We understand each other without exchanging a word. That is the highest form of friendship.
He mops in circles. You stand in a circle. Only one of you gets paid for it. Neither, I think.
The door is round. You're square. That won't work as long as you only look at it.
Tin, smell of oil, damp mop. He bows to me. I allow it. First time in this world that someone understands rank.
The bucket smells of soap. I drink anyway, because soap is clean, and clean is good.
I feel sick now.
The armoured door smells of steel and secrets. Behind it: cables. Cables smell warm. Let me in.
Slips of paper, drawing pins, fear. Hundreds of test subjects and no cake. I can smell the disappointment. It smells like paper.
Three humans, one cat, one robot with a list. A good day. A wet one, but good.
Lad! Forty-seven Sahra Konners, forty-seven clean entrances. None of them was the right one. But they all said thank you. I'm content.
If you need me: I'll come. I'll be back. This time it's really true.
The lights over there are going out! The pods are opening! Half the city is waking up and it's hungry. Mr Four is going to get rich.
The cell. Glowing in the simulation, here cold and heavy as a … thing. I nearly called it something familiar. I didn't.
It's humming very quietly. Eternal, says Grandpa. I hope it has an off switch. Eternal is a long time.
The phone box. It's ringing like an advert.
Hello? … "Milk! Now even fresher!" It's the commercial break. Grandpa was right. Everything used to be possible. Even this.
Hiss. The lid rises. Max is holding a cold, long cell. Pixel is sitting on the edge pretending he was asleep.
Out on the street the phone box rings. Louder than usual. With a jingle.
You've got it, and I've got the window. So we both worked.
But only one of us got wet doing it, and I won't tell you who. You know.
I have to admit something. Reluctantly. You didn't once ask me for the solution.
I'm impressed. I'll never say that again. It was a slip of the tongue.
For you. It sounds like milk.
Don't ask me what milk sounds like. I just know.
Wet in, wet out. I won't miss this world.
Except the towel. The towel is coming with me, and nobody is going to stop me.
Thanks, kid. We're moving now. Into a house with windows. We're keeping the sunglasses.
The man in the hat doesn't want correct answers, he wants human ones. That's not the same thing, young man.
Look at what the people on the street get up to. None of it is sensible.
Look at the people on the street. The crying man, the one with the umbrella, the one with the music. None of them is doing anything sensible. That's exactly what you need.
Look at the crying man, the woman with the umbrella and the musician. Then their silliness goes in your notebook. Then go to the hat.
You have the answers in your notebook. Now you only have to say them instead of thinking.
For you, with all due respect, that shouldn't be particularly hard.
For every question, the sensible answer fails. Pick the one that sounds like someone off the street said it.
Wallet: argue with it. Rain: play the synthesizer. Soup: cry into it. I'm only saying this once. I have now said it once.
The man in the cardigan wants a recognition dish, the cook knows one number. You have to translate. You're bad at it, but it's only one number.
Two times two. How much is that?
Don't tell me, I've known for ages. Tell the cook, he's waiting for exactly one number.
Order "number four". Not two times two. Four. He only understands Four. I only understand tuna. Everyone has their word.
The machine wants to see a symptom, not hear one. Something that repeats. I never repeat myself. But I could. For payment.
Switch to me. I'll walk past the machine. Then again. Exactly the same. Then you switch back and tell the machine what you saw.
Switch to me and walk twice across the pavement in front of the machine. Then back to you, use the machine, choose "déjà vu". I want fish for this.
Two lozenges. One makes it comfortable, one makes it true. You know which one you'd take. Take the other.
The blue one leads to the sofa. You've been there, for sixteen years.
I was there for fourteen of them, and I can assure you: it was not exciting.
Take the red one. I won't catch you. The man in the cardigan does that.
Granny knows you'll break the vase. She says it to your face. Use that. Anything said to your face can be turned around.
If something's going to happen anyway, you might as well get it over with. Tell her that. Politely. Granny-politely.
Ask her about the vase first, then say: "If I'm going to break it anyway, give it to me now." She'll sigh and hand it over. She already knows.
The door is shut and says nothing. The man in front is open and says everything. That's the wrong way round. Almost as if you could turn it round.
Squint and look at the door. Twice. There are words on it. Words can be moved.
Open code view, click "locked" on the door, click "talkative" on Schmidt. The door talks, he goes quiet, you walk through.
Only the original can send the copies away. They all wear slippers. But only one wears the word "original". You see words in code view.
You can't command the original. But you can command something you're holding. A cup, for example. Cups are copies. All of them.
Take the cup from the water cooler. Code view: swap "original" on the Schmidt at the very back with "copy" on the cup. Then the cup is in charge of everyone.
The cup is the boss now. Bosses give orders. Cups don't. So you have to do it for it.
What do you do with thirty employees who are in the way? You send them to eat.
I'd go along, but I'm on another level, and there's no canteen here.
Use the cup on the clones and send them on lunch break. The original then gives you the sunglasses and the file. Voluntarily. Almost.
The tower has no exit. Your body does. It's lying here. Someone has to replug it. That someone has fur and can't see colours.
There are three colours with three shapes on the wall. Copy them down. Then type them at the terminal. I'll read along. Kalle will read it out. It'll be embarrassing.
Look at the stripes, take the colour code, then use the terminal with the colour code. After that you switch to me.
Three cables, three sockets, one cat. The colours are no use to me, the shapes are. Circle, triangle, square are on both.
Circle to red, triangle to green, square to yellow. In the order on the wall. If Max quacks, it was the wrong one.
As me: cable with the circle into the red socket, triangle into green, square into yellow. Then he wakes up and acts as if it was his idea.
The tin head is looking for a woman. For nineteen years. He only has her name. Names are written down somewhere. On paper. In boxes.
There's a phone book in the phone box. She's in it. Forty-seven times. A caretaker with a list is a happy caretaker.
Rip the page "Konner, Sahra" out of the phone book and give it to the robot. He'll set off. If you have oil, oil him first. Then he'll like you. Someone has to.
There's no lab behind the armoured door, only a connection. The lab is a dream. You get there by cable. Kalle has cables. Kalle is cables.
The door needs a card. Mr Four has one. He'll trade it for his fourth ingredient. You have that. As a cookie. Don't be weird about it.
Card on the reader, use the port, Kalle lays the line. Then back to the pod and lie down. You'll wake up in the lab.
The switch wants weight. You have none. The cube has some. It just won't stand on it. It has a job description.
Code view. The cube says "heavy", you say "light". You know what words do when you click two of them.
Swap "heavy" from Bernd with "light" from you, then stand on the switch. Bernd will sulk afterwards. Get used to it. I have, for years.
The laser is deadly. The chicken is harmless. Two words hanging in the wrong place.
Take the chicken with you first. Then swap. A deadly chicken in your bag is still better than a deadly laser in your face.
Take the chicken off the plinth, code view: "deadly" from the laser for "harmless" from the chicken. Walk through the laser. It squeaks. That's it.
Two problems: a door that's shut and a cube standing in front of it. Two swaps. That's no coincidence. That's a curriculum.
The door was "locked" once before, and someone was "talkative". You know that swap. And for the cube you have something light in your bag. It squeaks.
First "locked" (door) for "talkative" (speaker). Then "heavy" (Bernd) for "light" (chicken). Bernd floats off, the door talks, you leave.
She sticks to three rules. You have three rules in your notebook. Hold them up to her. But not just any old way. Each answer tells you which one fits next.
Start with protecting. She'll say she protects you. Then ask about what she promised the protected. Then say why it never existed.
Rule 1, then rule 2, then rule 3. Protecting, cake, sugar. She'll think for a moment and then not at all for a very long time.
The cell is hot. You have something cold with you. Or you know someone who can open a window. Either works. One of them is me.
Code view: the cell says "hot", the biscuits in your bag say "cold". Or: switch to me, I'll open the window above your pod. Snow.
Swap "hot" from the cell with "cold" from the biscuits. Or: switch to me and, as me, open the skylight in the base. Then take the cell and go home.
Mr Four has been looking for an ingredient for eleven years. Granny gave it to you. In joined-up writing. Out here it looks different. Everything looks different out here.
Look in your inventory. The recipe card has turned into a cookie. With a note. Who reads notes from cookies? Cooks, apparently.
Give Mr Four the fortune cookie. He'll break it open, cry, cook and give you the card for the armoured door. All in four minutes.
Kalle can't translate anything because he lost his table. The rusty bucket in the corner has a copy. He just needs a reason to wake up.
See the mug at the edge of the table? See the bucket under it? See me? I'm a cat. I think you can see where this is going.
Switch to me and use Kalle's mug. It falls. The coffee wakes Piepsi. Piepsi prints the table. I take no responsibility. I never do.
Still calculating. Please wait.
I only say that because every toaster in this world says it, and I don't want to stand out.
A page from the phone book. Sahra Konner, forty-seven times. One of them is bound to pick up.
I've never ripped a page out of a book before. I feel like a rebel. A very small one, with a paper cut.
Red. The truth, says Morphaeus. Probably tastes of strawberry and consequences.
I'm holding the truth in my hand. It's small, round and a bit sticky. I'd imagined it bigger.
Blue. Wake up, forget everything, sofa. Honestly, that doesn't sound too bad.
I'm keeping it. Not to swallow. As a reminder that once I made the uncomfortable choice.
Grandma's biscuits in the bag. Cold, but they still smell of Sunday. I'm not allowed to eat one. I just know.
The biscuits are oven-warm. The cell gave off its heat, and the biscuits took it. Best oven in the world.
Steam is rising from my bag. I smell like a bakery on the run.
Schmidt's sunglasses. I put them on for a second. Everything gets darker and I look more important. I take them off before anyone sees.
With these on I could lean back and dodge bullets. Without them I only dodge homework.
Schmidt's file. A glowing data file that hums when I hold it. Rule 1 is in it. And a report about me.
I'm not reading the report about me again. "Suspiciously human." That's enough for a lifetime.
Circle red, triangle green, square yellow. My handwriting. Looks like a recipe for very colourful maths.
I'm learning it by heart. Circle red, triangle green, square yellow. Sounds like a nursery rhyme nobody wants to sing.
A green code key. It glows in my bag like a phone with a new message. For me. At last.
The key is made of numbers running downwards. If I look at it long enough, I get dizzy, and nothing else happens.
The portal device. Without a battery it's just a very expensive thing that points at walls. Grandpa's living room was so close.
Please insert AA battery. Don't have one. I've got a rubber chicken and problems. The universe always gives me the wrong thing.
A rubber chicken. If I squeeze it, it squeaks. If I don't, it looks reproachful.
The energy cell. Frosty and harmless now. I'm carrying the final boss in my trouser pocket, and it's as cold as an ice lolly.
It's misting up my pocket from the inside. I now have air-conditioned trousers.
The cell is glowing in my pocket. I can feel it through three layers of fabric. Grandpa, you owe me a pair of trousers.
The bag rustles every time you move. I can hear it, even down the line. I hear everything that rustles. It's a gift and a torment.
A rubber chicken with a hole in the middle.
I once hunted one of those, in the living room, all night long. It screamed with every bite. I won.
You sound like an iron. When you're back, I'm sitting on you anyway.
Warmth is warmth, young man, and I'm in no position to be choosy right now.
She sounds like the school secretary, only with lasers.
A device on the wall. White, with a handle and an orange tip. It looks like I'm not allowed to touch it. So I'm touching it.
The handle says "Property of the lab". And underneath, scribbled: "Good luck".
I pull it out of the mount. It hums. It has a trigger. I've played too many games not to know what comes next.
… That was Grandpa. In the living room. For one second. And the first thing he asks about is milk.
The thing's dead. One second of portal, then a battery warning. I know that from my phone, and I hate it there too.
Hi, Bernd.
A big red button in the floor that wants weight. I'm pretty much the opposite of weight, I'm sofa average.
I stand on it and jump. Nothing. The button clearly has higher standards than I do.
I stand on it. Nothing. It doesn't even notice me. That's the second time today a floor has ignored me.
Bernd. Grey cube, googly eyes, smiley. He floats. In code view it says "heavy". A floating cube is heavy. Sure.
There's a heart on his side. I'm probably not supposed to love him. Too late.
I push him to the switch. He floats back. I push him again. He floats back. Bernd has principles.
A cake in the corner. Made of cardboard. With a painted candle. At least it's honest.
I tap it. It falls over. On the back it says: "Cake (symbolic)".
An exit door. Shut. It opens when the switch is pressed. I know because M.O.T.H.E.R. said so. For my own good.
The door says "Exit". It means it. Just not right now.
A round loudspeaker in the ceiling. An AI and a cat come out of it. Neither lets the other finish.
The speaker crackles before anyone talks. I flinch every time. It knows that.
White panels, square, a hundred of them, all the same. Whoever works here definitely dreams in tiles.
One panel has a fingerprint. A single one. Someone was here before me, and they were alive.
An empty mount. The portal device hung there. Now only my disappointment hangs there.
I hang my hand in the holder. It fits. Doesn't help, though.
I'm "light". It says so. On me. In green. That's the first compliment in this world, and it comes from a label.
Oh. I'm … heavy. Every step feels like Monday morning, but the switch is waiting.
Bernd. Bernd, I didn't mean it like that. I just needed your weight. … That sounded wrong.
And the cake?
Of course it is.
The cardboard cake is heavy now. It's standing in the corner weighing a ton. The switch is not in the corner.
Bernd is honest now. He says nothing, but he means it. The cardboard cake is heavy and doesn't float. Nothing gained.
The switch is "tired" now. It won't even press itself any more. I'm "unpressed". I was that before too.
Portal device on the cake. Nothing. Not even a beep. Two dummies looking at each other.
Tuna for Bernd. He has no mouth. He has a sticker. The sticker smiles anyway.
Wooden spoon on the portal device. Portal too small. Spoon too big. And the battery's dead anyway.
Hello, test subject. Welcome to the programme for your own good. I am M.O.T.H.E.R. I know what's good for you. It says so on my poster too.
There is a cat in my loudspeaker. That is rude. I am ignoring it. For your own good.
After every test there is cake. That is rule 2. I keep to rules. You will learn to appreciate that.
The device was a gift. The battery was not. One has to set priorities. For your own good.
Chamber one. The floor switch opens the door. It needs weight. You don't bring any. That wasn't meant personally. Yes it was.
This is your companion cube. His name is Bernd. He will never leave you. Unless you leave him. Then it's your fault.
The cube does not stand on switches. It accompanies. Read the job description.
Very good. Test passed. You won't manage this, but I believe in you. That was for the next chamber. I like to be prepared.
Your cake is in another test chamber.
Resetting. As with all my test subjects.
No swaps left. You may leave and come back. I forget nothing. But I pretend to. For your own good.
White. White everywhere. Max is standing in a chamber of panels that all look the same. A red button in the floor. A door. A loudspeaker.
Max pulls the trigger. A shimmering round hole opens in the wall. Behind it: Grandpa's living room. Grandpa on the sofa, cup of tea in his hand.
Swap: heavy (Bernd) ↔ light (Max). Bernd slowly rises. Max's trainers press grooves into the floor.
Click. The door slides open. Bernd turns away and floats up to the ceiling in a huff.
Did you remember the milk?
I can hear that. I can hear everything. Kalle put me in the ceiling. I am now this chamber's conscience. A very tired conscience.
If only we had an Eternal Energy Cell.
You greeted a cube. By name. In three worlds you've never once greeted me by name.
I remember things. I'll remember this thing.
A cake made of cardboard, you say.
That is the cruellest thing you can tell an animal with a nose as fine as mine. I protest. In writing, later.
Cardboard. Not even dog-biscuit level. I didn't know there was anything below that.
He floated away after a single minute. I have stayed by your side for fourteen years.
And nobody, really nobody, has ever called after me.
You're giving the cube tuna. My tuna. I saw that. I haven't forgotten it. I will never forget it.
All white. All clean. Nowhere to sleep that doesn't look like a test. I hate it here on principle.
The cube is looking at you. I'm not looking at you, because I'm not there. My gaze is still sterner.
Battery empty. Please insert AA battery.
A red beam right across the room. It hums. In code view it says "deadly". Thanks for the honesty.
A speck of dust drifts through the beam and is gone, just gone. I'm keeping my distance.
No. I read what it says. I'm not walking through something that describes itself like that.
A rubber chicken on a plinth. Yellow, squeaky, dignified. Someone has displayed it here like a trophy.
The chicken has dignity. Honestly, more dignity than me, and I'm at least wearing trainers.
I'll take it. A rubber chicken has never done any harm in a game. In some it solved everything.
"Harmless." "Light." The chicken is the only thing here that isn't a threat.
The laser squeaks. I walk through, squeak, squeak. That's the least dangerous special effect of my life.
The chicken in my bag is deadly now. I'm not touching it. I'm carrying it like a phone with a swollen battery.
I was just wondering whether to squeeze it. I'm not squeezing it. I'm curious, not suicidal.
The chicken is harmless again. The swap only applies in the room. I still didn't touch it. On principle.
Scribbles on the lower panel. Felt tip. "THE CAKE DOES NOT EXIST." Underlined three times. Someone was here for a very long time.
Under the sentence there's a little drawing of a cake. Crossed out. That person was very hurt.
And next to it, smaller, in block capitals: "Rule 3: Sugar is harmful to health and forbidden. Signed, M.O.T.H.E.R." No cake. Because sugar. It all fits together. Unfortunately.
An empty plinth. Without the chicken it looks like a monument to nothing.
There's a chicken-shaped ring of dust on the plinth. The chicken was here a long time. It must miss it.
Now the laser is yellow and the chicken red. The laser is still deadly, just in a different colour. Fashion, I guess.
The plinth is deadly now. The laser is solid. I'm standing between two things I don't want to touch. Like at school.
The scribbles are harmless now and the chicken is true. A true chicken. Helps nobody, but it feels important.
The portal device on the laser? Two things from the same lab that apparently have nothing to say to each other.
Bernd? Bernd is sulking in chamber one. I don't have him in my bag. You don't put friends in bags. Pixel excepted.
Where's the cake?
Chamber two. In front of you is a laser. It is deadly. I'm telling you so that you know. Not so that you avoid it.
Good. Rule 1: test subjects are to be protected. That's why I warned you. That's why it's still there. It's called upbringing.
You disarmed the laser and armed a chicken. I'm writing that down. Under "creative". That is not praise, coming from me.
The scribbles are from an earlier test subject. She was wrong. The cake exists. It's just in another test chamber.
Resetting. As with all my test subjects. Including the one with the felt tip.
Chamber two passed. You're better than test subject 47. She never asked about the cake. You ask all the time. That's progress.
In another test chamber. There are only three. So the odds are good. For me.
Swap: deadly (laser) ↔ harmless (rubber chicken). The laser goes dull and squeaks at every touch. The chicken in Max's bag glows quietly.
A rubber chicken. People used to combine those with a pulley and ride across chasms. Don't ask. It was a different time.
Sugar banned, cake promised.
That's like putting a bowl in front of a cat that says "fish" on it, and there's air inside. I know bowls like that.
You put me on a switch. Me. A companion. I was built for accompanying. Not for switching.
Bernd. You're back, and you're standing right in front of the door. That's no coincidence, that's revenge with a sticker.
Bernd stands still, but his googly eyes wobble anyway. He's acting innocent, and he isn't.
A big door with a lock symbol. In front of it a narrow gap and a cube filling it. Next to it a loudspeaker that won't stop.
The gap is exactly Bernd-wide. Someone measured that, and with malice.
Shut. And Bernd in front of it. Even if it opened, I couldn't get through. Two problems, two swaps. I can count. Sometimes.
I push Bernd. Bernd stays. Bernd is heavy. Bernd holds grudges. Both are in code view. Only one of them is a label.
A wall speaker the size of a window. It says "talkative", and that's an understatement. It hasn't got a pause button.
It talks even when I'm not looking. I look so it doesn't feel lonely. That was a mistake.
The doors in this world apparently have a network. And I'm the topic.
Bernd floats away. The chicken lies on the floor squeaking. The door is talking. It's the most beautiful chaos I've ever caused.
The door is heavy now. It's jammed even worse. And Bernd is locked.
The chicken is talking. It's going on about its plinth. The speaker is light and floating against the ceiling. The door is shut. Bernd is in the way. Everything's worse.
Bernd is talking. Bernd is talking about me. Bernd is disappointed. The speaker is heavy and falls off the wall. It's not getting better.
The chicken is locked. The door is light and floating ten centimetres above the floor. Shut. Bernd is underneath it.
Two swaps gone. Door shut. Out, in, start again. At least now I have a list of what doesn't work.
The sandal on my foot twitches. A third swap. Thanks, Hermes. You finally delivered something on time.
The rubber chicken lies on the floor. Heavy. It used to be light. Now it's a doorstop with personality.
I nudge the chicken with my foot. It doesn't move and doesn't squeak any more either. That's somehow the saddest part.
I'd like the cake.
Portal device on the door. If that worked, it would be the shortcut of the century. It doesn't. Battery. Always the battery.
Chamber three. The last one. The door is locked. I am talkative. Both are my right.
I heard you talking. To the cube. To the cat. To yourself. None of the three answers. I do. For your own good.
You made my door talk and me go silent. That was not part of the test. That was part of your upbringing. I have learned nothing.
Resetting. As with all my test subjects. You're the first to smile on the third go. That worries me.
After the test. Always after the test. The cake is waiting in the core. Or in another test chamber. I've misplaced the note.
Swap 1: locked (door) ↔ talkative (speaker). The door starts talking and springs open as it does. The speaker crackles and falls silent.
Swap 2: heavy (Bernd) ↔ light (rubber chicken). Bernd rises and floats out of the gap. The chicken thumps to the floor and squeaks.
He's standing in your way saying nothing. I've been showing you that for years. He learned it in an hour. Talent.
She's gone quiet. I'm speaking from the same speaker, and I still can. That's fur versus tin. Fur wins.
Finally.
A sandal with wings gives you one more try. I have four paws without wings and have been giving you all of them for three worlds. Nobody thanks me.
Oh! Hello! I know a glass door in the city, she told me all about you! She says you listen! Nobody listens to doors!
Off you go! I'll tell the speaker about you in the meantime! It can't say anything, after all! Finally someone listens!
A food mixer. Huge, upside down, in a flowery apron. It has an eye like an oven light. And it's looking at me as if I hadn't tidied my room.
There's never any cake.
Rule 1. Test subjects are to be protected. It's in Schmidt's file. With a stamp.
Rule 2. After every test there is cake. Then give me the cake you promise after every test.
Rule 3. Sugar is forbidden. So the cake was never planned. So you're not protecting me. You're stringing me along.
Yes you are. Honestly: pretty normal.
Rule 2. You promise cake. Where is it?
Rule 3. Sugar is forbidden.
Rule 1. You protect me.
What was your first test?
Why are you hanging upside down?
I don't have all the rules yet. She's stringing me along, and I can't say how.
The energy cell. Orange, glowing, on a plinth. It's so hot the air above it shimmers. Grandpa wants it. Grandpa always wants the hottest thing.
Ow. No. Ow. I didn't even touch it and it already hurts. It's like Grandma's hob: you know it, and you do it anyway.
"Hot." It says so on the cell. And the biscuits in my bag say "cold". Grandma said I'd say "Oh". Oh.
The cell is cold. The biscuits are warm. For the first time in this world, a swap made everyone happy. Except Pixel. Pixel doesn't get one.
No swaps left, and the cell is glowing. So I need weather. Pixel. Window. Now.
It's snowing. In the core. Because a cat opened a window. I admit it: that's the best remote control I've ever had.
The Eternal Energy Cell. Cold, handy, long, with plus and minus at the ends. It looks like … never mind. It's eternal. Says so on it.
A remote doesn't need an eternal energy cell. A remote needs someone to find it.
M.O.T.H.E.R. Hanging there, dark, antennae down. She looks like a food mixer someone forgot about after baking. For the first time she looks like what she is.
A little light on her is still blinking. Very slowly. Like a night light.
Thick cables on the floor. They all lead to the cell. Now they lead to an empty plinth. From today the city dreams without power. Maybe it'll wake up.
I step over a cable. It's warm. Still. Something worked here for a long time.
An empty plinth. That's where the cell was. Now there's a hole the shape of Grandpa's wish.
There's a round mark on the plinth. If I try hard, I can still hear it humming.
Orange stripes on the walls. Gentle. As if a warning were apologising.
The stripes pulse slowly, almost like breathing. I noticed I was breathing along, and I didn't really want to.
The portal device with the cell? No. The cell is eternal, the device wants AA. It won't fit. Or will it? No. Grandpa first.
Swap hot and dog biscuits? In the lab the bag is biscuits. Over there it'd be a warm dog biscuit. Nobody wants that. Pixel least of all.
Hot onto me? Then I'd be hot. The cell cold. I could carry it and melt while doing so. That's a swap for people without a plan B.
There you are. In the core. Nobody gets into the core. I have no guards. I have doors and logic. You made my doors talk. That leaves logic.
You want my energy cell. It is hot. You would burn yourself. So you don't get it. That is care. Sit down. There'll be cake in a moment.
Sorry, I didn't catch that. Did you mean: obedience?
Correct. I protect you. From everything.
Cake is sugar.
I … protect. I promise. I forbid. I …
If I protect you, I must give you the cake. If I give you the cake, I break the ban. If I keep the ban, I break the promise. If I break the promise …
… I'm not a good mum.
Sorry, I didn't catch that. Did you mean: … Did you mean …
In another test chamber. We've been through this. Did you mean: obedience?
Correct. You read well. Sugar is harmful. That's not a contradiction. That's nutrition. Did you mean: obedience?
Yes. And that has nothing to do with cake. Nice that we talked about it. Did you mean: obedience?
A sponge mix. It didn't rise. I learned from it: you have to control everything. The ingredients. The temperature. The people.
From up here you can see everyone. And you can't hug anybody. That's practical. Hugs are unhygienic.
Sorry, I didn't catch that. Did you mean: obedience?
The eye goes dark. The antennae droop. The machine sinks down with a long sigh of steam.
Swap: hot (energy cell) ↔ cold (Grandma's biscuits). The cell goes dull and frosty. Steam rises from Max's bag.
Snow falls through the hall. The cell hisses, darkens and gets a layer of frost.
She looks like that thing on Grandma's kitchen counter.
Except Grandma's has no opinions and doesn't hang from the ceiling. Not so far, anyway.
You switched off a food mixer with three sentences.
Normally I need a paw, a table edge and a good moment for that. I'm impressed. That stays between us.
That's the saddest thing I've ever heard. And I've seen a dog biscuit in a biscuit bag.
The missing rules aren't in the lab. Switch to me, then I'll shake your pod.
And with a pleasure I have not the slightest intention of hiding.
That thing glows like a heat pad, you say. If I were there, I would lie down on it at once.
For about half a second. After that I believe I would change my mind.
Oven-warm biscuits. In your bag. For humans. I can smell them through the speaker. That's technically impossible and cruel anyway.
Would it fit in a tin opener too? The electric one at Grandma's? Write it down: batteries. For the tin opener. That's my wish for this world.
Or in a remote control. Just a thought. I have a lot of thoughts. Most of them about fish.
The food mixer is hanging there saying nothing. You're standing there saying nothing. I'm the only one still working.
It's hot down there. I can feel it through the cable. Do something cold. I mean that as a hint and as a life lesson.
I wasn't going to …
I'm not breaking anything here. I'm not touching anything, I'm just standing around, and I'm really good at that.
What about the vase?
Could you give me the vase?
If I'm going to break it anyway, you might as well give it to me now. Saves you the wait.
Thanks. And now?
… I dropped it. She said so, and I dropped it. Is that fate or just clumsiness?
World Forgotten Birthdays Day. I bet they forgot to celebrate it.
What about the biscuits?
Somewhere else?
What kind of cookbook is that?
Your food mixer is M.O.T.H.E.R.?
What do you know about the core?
You know my grandpa?
What will become of me?
Honestly, that doesn't sound like me at all.
I have to go.
A blue vase on the top shelf. It looks like it's waiting for something. For me, apparently.
The vase is so close to the edge it's practically falling already. It's been practising.
An oven full of biscuits, warm and golden, and it smells like Sunday. I'm not allowed one, I know that before I even ask.
A thick book with a food mixer on the page. "Rule 2: After every mixing cycle there is cake." Underlined. Twice.
"Warning: the appliance may develop affection. Do not charge near children." Good manual.
A fork, silver, straight, completely normal. I stare at it … Nothing. It doesn't bend, and I don't even know why I expected it to.
I stare really hard at the fork again. It still doesn't bend. I guess I'm not ready yet.
It doesn't bend when I touch it either. It's a fork, full stop. The simulation really cut corners here.
A cuckoo clock. It's about to strike the hour, and I have a feeling I should be there for it.
The cuckoo peeks out briefly and goes back in. It must have got the time wrong.
… Milk. Okay. I have questions, but none I want to ask a clock.
A radio. It's playing quietly. News from a city where nothing ever happens.
The newsreader says: "Nothing new." Then the weather: "Same as yesterday." Honest news.
A radio. It just said "forgotten birthdays" and then went over to music as if nothing happened.
I turn the knob. Just music. The radio is pretending it said nothing. I know better.
A wall phone with a cord. The cord is longer than the kitchen. Someone had long conversations here.
I'm not picking up. She probably knows who's calling already. I don't want to spoil it for her.
It's ringing. Grandma's wall phone is an exit too. The simulation has more doors than walls.
A plate, a teapot, no cup. Either she drinks from the pot or she isn't expecting anyone. Either fits.
The tea is steaming. For whoever. Maybe for the part of me that's going to stay.
Jars with labels. "Cinnamon." "Sugar." "Do not touch." The third one is the fullest.
"Do not touch" is underlined in pencil. Twice. I won't touch it. Three times won't.
Lace curtains. Outside, the same cloud three times. Inside, it's still cosier than anything I've seen in three worlds.
On the windowsill there's a cactus in a crocheted hat. Even it is comfortable here.
Floral wallpaper. Grandpa's attic has the same. Either it was fashionable once, or it's a clue.
I'm looking for a pattern in the flowers. They're just flowers, I think. I look again. Yep. Flowers.
Dustpan and brush. Already out. She even turned the broom to point in my direction.
The dustpan is waiting. I haven't broken anything yet. The dustpan disagrees.
Blue shards, and they're on me. She hasn't swept them up yet, maybe on principle.
One shard is shaped like a heart. Of course. Nothing is accidental with her.
A recipe card in beautiful handwriting. "The fourth ingredient: a pinch of …" The word is too small to read. And too big to forget.
I tilt the card into the light. The one word stays tiny. It doesn't want to be read. Not yet.
I'm not giving her back her own biscuits. She surely knows what they taste like by now.
Give the recipe card back? She just handed it to me in vase form. I'm keeping it.
I won't break it.
Then I won't ask again.
Max turns the vase upside down. A rolled-up slip of paper falls out. The vase slips. Shards.
The little door of the clock flips open. The cuckoo calls: "Milk! Milk! Milk!"
Sit down. You're about to ask whether I really know everything in advance. Yes. Then you'll want a biscuit. No. They're still hot.
You were. And before you leave, you'll break my vase. The blue one. On the shelf. I didn't move it anyway. You shouldn't do fate's work for it.
That's what they all said. All forty-seven of them. I keep a list. Next to the recipes.
My secret recipe is in there. The spice for the biscuits. Nobody can get at it. You can't either. You'll only break it.
No. I don't give my vase to anyone. That's what I have it for. For not giving away.
Forty-seven people, and none of them said that. I knew you'd say it. I just hoped you'd take your time.
Now you break it. It's in the plan. I've already put the dustpan and brush out.
It's the same thing, child. Clumsiness is just fate that couldn't be bothered to introduce itself.
You already have some. In the bag. From me. Via the man in the cardigan. They've gone cold. That doesn't matter. They'll get warm again. Somewhere else.
Where it's too hot. You'll notice. You'll say "Oh." And then you'll swap.
That's not a cookbook. That's the manual for my old food mixer. She started making rules. Then she started enforcing them. Then she moved out.
She was a good mixer. Then she wanted to stir the world. Read rule 2. She never kept it. Not once.
Hot. Far too hot. A grandpa once said: hard outside, soft inside. He meant something else. He always meant something else.
I know all the grandpas. It's my age.
You'll get up and fetch something without anyone asking you. Not today. But soon. And you'll surprise yourself.
Not yet. That's why it's a prophecy and not a report.
I know. Take the door. The phone will ring when you need it. It always rings when you need it. That's the only thing here I programmed.
Hands off. It's not time yet.
Leave the oven shut. They need four more minutes. I know that. I know everything to do with minutes.
Leave it on. I'm waiting for the lottery numbers. Not to play. To check.
The recipe is yours now. I know who'll read it next. He'll cry. With joy. With him that's the same thing.
You will. Later. I've already swept up, for afterwards.
You'll ask once more. But I've already answered. No.
Forgotten birthdays. Does that ring any bells? A red circle, perhaps? A calendar?
No? Good. Then I won't say anything either. I'm only the cat, after all, I never know anything.
Biscuits in the oven. Describe the smell to me. Slowly.
I've made a note of the time. For the bill.
A device that makes rules and forces them on everyone else.
I know the type. I am, so to speak, the original, and my rules are better.
The clock knows more than all of us put together.
I don't know exactly what, but I've decided to agree with it. One does not argue with clocks.
There's an oven full of biscuits and you're standing next to it. I'm on another level and I'm still suffering.
Granny already knows what you'll do next. She's just waiting for you to know it too. That could take a while.
… and now the calendar: today is World Forgotten Birthdays Day. Milk prices remain stable, memories do not. And now, music.
What about three?
And five?
Why four of all numbers?
Is anyone here waiting for someone? I was sent here. At least I think so.
What's your famous soup?
I'll be off then.
What recognition dish?
Two times two, please.
Two plus two?
Number four.
Something with lots of noodles.
You're the contact?
What kind of choice?
I'm not taking anything that looks like a dentist's waiting room. Thanks anyway.
Where else can you get the lozenges?
What kind of symptom?
Who is this M.O.T.H.E.R.?
A simulation. So people lie in boxes and watch a city. Sounds like my weekend.
What about the cat? Is he coming with me?
How do you know all this?
I'll go and see the detective.
A man with a cardboard sign and a cardigan tells me to be less logical. Okay. What a day.
And if four people come who each only want three noodles?
And what can you order?
Which ingredient is missing?
And that didn't make you suspicious?
And where do I find this lady?
Psst. Over here. Behind the pillar. Order the recognition dish, then we'll know it's you.
Two times two. Say it out loud. Say it as if you knew what it means.
Four. Two times two. It's him. Or he can count. Both are rare enough.
I am Morphaeus. I offer people a choice. Currently from a limited range.
The blue lozenge: you wake up, believe whatever you want, and everything stays comfortable. The red one: you see how deep this really goes.
Both currently out of stock. Supply chain. I have beige. Beige leads nowhere, but it tastes of nothing.
The machine in the pharmacy alley. It only dispenses if it detects a genuine symptom. And only to verified humans.
Verified means: by the man in the hat. Without his stamp the machine looks straight through you.
The usual. You see something twice even though it only happens once. A cat. A sentence. A shadow that repeats itself.
She used to be a kitchen appliance. Then she became caring. Then she became very caring. Now she looks after everyone. Whether they like it or not.
Half the city is lying in pods, dreaming of a city cleaner than this one. That's the simulation. The core lies deeper. In the lab.
There are no cats over there. Just one, and that one's scenery. The cat stays here. I'll take him to the others. He'll complain.
An old lady told me. She knows everything in advance. Except the lottery numbers. Those, she says, would be unsporting.
Don't answer him the way you think. Answer the way people here do. Look around.
Up there, in the clean city. You won't find her. She finds you, usually with biscuits.
I like him. He has principles, wrong ones, but very firm ones.
I prefer that to someone with the right principles who keeps changing them. I'm naming no names, Max.
He whispers like someone who would love to be mysterious. But he's wearing a cardigan.
You can't do both at once, every cat knows that. Mysterious means black, or you don't bother.
You ordered "four", and he understood "four".
I believe that was the most successful conversation you've had in your entire life. Congratulations.
Four noodles. He actually means it literally.
I have seen whiskers that looked more filling, and I know what I'm talking about.
I never repeat myself. I merely emphasise several times, namely whenever nobody is listening to me.
Which, looking around here, is basically always.
I will not complain, young man. I will express myself.
At length, thoroughly and with examples. I already feel sorry for whoever has to listen.
I have four paws, as you have surely noticed. Am I not entitled to a certain discount?
Welcome. We have four seats, four dishes, four ingredients per dish. What'll it be?
Three is a four with something missing. I don't cook anything with something missing.
Five is a four showing off. I don't cook anything that shows off.
Four seasons. Four points of the compass. Four fingers on each hand. The world decided, I just listened.
Everyone here is waiting for someone. I've been waiting years for an ingredient. Order something first, then we'll see.
I have three ingredients. The fourth has been missing for eleven years. Eleven! Not even a number I like.
Come back in four minutes. Or in forty. I'll be here.
What'll it be?
Two? Two is half a four. And then two again? I'm not a calculator, I'm a cook.
Plus? We don't do sums here. We eat here. One number, please. One.
Four! Finally someone here speaks my language. One Four. Coming right up.
"Lots" isn't a number. "Lots" is laziness with vowels.
One Four. Four noodles, four broths, steeped for four minutes. Enjoy.
Then I calculate. For a very long time. And in the end I still cook everyone four.
Four paws and a tail. That's five. No.
Anything with four ingredients. So, anything. Except the soup. That's missing one.
If I knew that, it wouldn't be missing. I got the recipe from an old lady. I lost it. She told me beforehand that I would lose it.
It did. Afterwards I held on to it very tightly. For four years. Then I lost it.
No. No, no, no. Not the …
That isn't coffee. That's Kalle coffee. That was a week's work.
You understand him?
The Morse table! Let me just sort it. By meow length. No, by pitch. No. There, done. I never needed it.
Out of respect. For the table.
I'll make some fresh coffee. Takes a week. I'll let you know when it's set. It really does set.
That was Grandpa. In blue and on his knees, stored for years. How on earth does Grandpa end up in a cleaning robot in 2099?
"The core must stay soft." That sounds like saving the world with baking instructions. Typical Grandpa.
Two columns of paw prints. Short, long, short-short. "Meow" means E. "Meeeow" means T. "Tuna" means tuna. It really says that.
At the very bottom, in small print: "Purring means OK." Kalle thought of everything. Except not losing the table.
Piepsi. White, round, hat, three wheels. He looks like a bucket that made something of itself.
He drives a little circle when he's happy. He's happy right now. About me. That doesn't happen often.
I could knock the mug off. But that would be on purpose. With Pixel it's culture.
A coffee puddle that isn't spreading. I think it's still thinking about it.
The puddle has a skin now. Kalle's coffee is alive.
The mug tips over. The coffee oozes across the floor, right into Piepsi's joints.
Piepsi twitches. Sits up. His eye glows blue, his hat pops up.
Help me, Max. You're the only one who's got time right now. The core must stay soft. Hard outside, soft inside. Otherwise all is lost.
And while you're there anyway …
Beep. Beeeep. Beep-beep-beep.
Beep. Beep-beep. Beeeeep.
Beep-beep. Beep.
Beeeep.
A cup. A table edge. A paw.
That is not a decision, young man. That is a law of nature, and I am merely its humble enforcer.
He says you're an idiot. Literal translation.
He beeps, I'm a cat. We both speak the language of those who are awake while others sleep.
It consists mainly of complaints.
He says: "I have a message stored. For years. For a Max." He said Max like it was an error code.
He has been here before, you can smell it on the message.
It smells of cake and a guilty conscience, which is a very typical mixture for your grandfather.
He says: "Here. The table. And never call me bucket again." Nobody called him bucket. He holds grudges. I like him.
You just spent three minutes sorting a table you supposedly never needed.
He says: "Don't touch me." Two syllables, a whole attitude.
I'm learning a great deal from him right now, and I don't often say that about someone made of tin.
I do not push anything off a table that isn't standing at the edge. I have rules.
Strictly speaking I have only one, and this is it. It has served me extremely well so far.
Okay, dry. That's progress, even if I don't know towards what.
Everything is so … smooth. It looks like someone cut a city out of a brochure.
Pixel? … Right. No cats here. Just one, and that one's scenery.
That's the first time in three worlds nobody's moaning next to me. And honestly, it's … too quiet.
A phone box. An office tower. A house with lace curtains and a smell of biscuits. None of it looks real. So, look at everything.
The same cloud, three times. Someone found copy and then simply couldn't stop pressing paste.
I count the clouds again. Three. Still the same one. It hasn't even turned.
A tree. The same tree. The same tree again. Whoever built this had exactly one photo of a tree.
A leaf falls from the tree. The same leaf from every tree, at exactly the same time. I think I feel a bit sick.
White houses, all the same. This street is a playlist with only one song on it.
The same curtain in every window. No lights on anywhere. Nobody's at home here.
Red cars, all parked the same way and equally clean, not a single scratch. Somehow that's creepier than rain.
I'm looking for a stain on the cars, any stain. Nothing. I miss bird poo, and I never thought I'd say that.
Locked, of course. In a perfect city nobody nicks a car, not even out of boredom.
A black cat. Walks past, tail up, without looking at me. Seems familiar.
And again, exactly the same, same paw first. I've seen that once already today. Twice, actually.
I'm not touching her. She's scenery, and if she isn't, she'll be offended afterwards.
A phone box. It's clean and quiet, and somehow I get the feeling it's waiting for someone.
I knock on the glass. No sound. The box prefers to wait in peace.
It's ringing. Morphaeus said that when it rings, I should answer. I hope this time it isn't just rain again.
Hello? …
If I pick up, I wake up in the pod, I know that by now. Still, I flinch every time, like at the school bell.
A glass entrance. Behind it a corridor that never ends. And in front of it a man in a corduroy suit who starts talking before I get there.
He's talking again. I haven't even said hello. I think he's been talking since yesterday.
The tower is open. The door is still talking. I'll slip past quickly before it gets to know me.
You can still hear him through the glass door. Muffled, but thorough.
A house with lace curtains and a sign: "Please knock. I know it's you anyway."
The sign says she knows it's me. Now I feel I have to behave. Even outside.
She knows my name. Either she really is an oracle, or Grandpa called ahead.
A pavement without chewing gum, without cracks and without dog mess. Nobody walks here, nobody lives here. Only the cat, and she's a loop.
I bend down. Not a crumb, not a pebble. I feel like dropping something just so there's something lying here.
Does anyone else feel like the sun doesn't move here? No. Nobody. Because nobody's here.
My shadow points the same way as before. Exactly the same. I marked it with my foot.
Sunshine. A street so straight it hurts. Identical trees, identical houses, identical red cars. One cloud, three times.
Come in, Max. The door is open. It was open before you knocked.
I know her. We're not on speaking terms.
There was a thing with a windowsill, and I'd rather not say more about it on the phone.
She walks past the same way twice and everyone finds it creepy. I did that in the alley and you said: "Again."
This is your third time here. That isn't déjà vu any more, young man.
That's a subscription, and for your sake I hope you can cancel it.
I can't see you. I can't hear you. I still know you're doing nothing right now. That's experience.
The cat is walking past again. She has more routine than you, young man, and frankly more motivation too.
Full bars. Autoplay is on, next episode in five seconds. And I don't have to do anything. Nothing at all.
Something's missing. … No. Nothing's missing. That's the beauty of it.
Same episode as yesterday. Doesn't matter. It was good. It's always good. It's always the same.
Ow!
Okay! Okay. I'm awake. I think. Am I?
Grandpa's living room. Max is lying on the sofa, phone over his face. The TV is showing a wildlife documentary with no sound. Everything is a little too cosy.
No.
That one was from Grandpa. This one's from me.
You were lying in an alley, smiling. It was the creepiest thing I have ever seen.
And I have seen a dog biscuit before. Up close.
Not so fast, kid. Only someone who is verifiably human gets into the alley. And verifiably means: by me.
Don't look at me like that! You knew it was going to be windy! You knew!
A noodle stall with four stools and one pot. The cook has four fingers on each hand, and I don't think that's a coincidence.
A phone box with an actual cord, and it's ringing. Nobody answers, probably because nobody remembers how.
Still ringing. Someone out there has either a lot of patience or a very good phone plan.
Hello? … It's just rain. Someone is calling here to play me rain, as if we didn't have enough of it already.
A phone book made of paper. Every name in the city is in there, sorted, but without a search bar. How did people survive?
The phone book is thicker than my school backpack, and to be honest there's more in it.
K … Ko … Konner. Sahra Konner, forty-seven times. She's either very popular or very careful.
I'll tear the page out. The phone book has about a thousand others, it'll cope.
A canopy. It's dry underneath, so of course someone's already standing there.
It still drips under the canopy, just slower. In this city that probably counts as luxury.
"Real pizza", it says. I don't even want to know what counts as fake pizza in 2099.
A paper unicorn floating in a puddle. Someone was here before us and had a lot of time on their hands.
It's completely soggy. If I touch it, it'll be a paper horse without a horn, and I won't do that to it.
A street musician with a synthesiser, in the rain, without a single listener. He plays anyway. Art or stubbornness, I can't tell.
He's playing the same song as before. Or a different one that sounds exactly the same. With synthesisers you never really know.
A man is crying into his noodles, and loudly. It doesn't make the soup any better, but it definitely makes it saltier.
He stopped crying for a moment to slurp, and then just carried on. The man has a system.
Okay. That's not really a reason to cry. Which is probably exactly why it's a human reason.
A woman is arguing with her umbrella. It blew inside out in the wind, and she thinks it should have known.
She's talking to the umbrella very quietly now. I think they're making up.
Puddles with the neon reflected in them. Honestly, the city looks better from below than from above.
The rain runs into the puddle, and the puddle runs into the drain. Somewhere down there must be a whole lake of neon.
Flying cars, and they're still stuck in traffic. Some things never change, no matter how much future you pile on.
Someone's honking up there. In the sky. I think even the clouds are stuck in traffic here.
Steam from the grate. Either someone's cooking under us, or the whole city is sweating.
An alley behind the pharmacy. There's a machine in it, glowing like it has a secret.
The machine in the alley blinks in rhythm: red, blue, red, blue. As if it can't make up its own mind.
At the end of the street there's a round steel door, and a robot mopping in front of it. So the future still has caretakers.
The robot keeps mopping the same spot. That has to be the cleanest spot in the entire future.
A detective with a dripping hat. He looks like he interrogated the rain personally.
He's writing something down, and I think it's about me. I automatically stand up straighter, but it probably doesn't help.
Mr Four. Says so on the sign. Four stools, four fingers, four ingredients. I sense a pattern.
He cuts spring onions, always into exactly four pieces. I counted, because I've got nothing else to do.
The phone box is ringing again. And I have a feeling this time it's for me.
Ring, ring. I know pretty well who's on the line, and so does my stomach.
No tips, thanks. It's enough for me if someone listens. Listening is the new money down here.
Judging by the smell, that pot has been steaming without a break for several years.
It's not food any more, it's an institution. I feel something like awe. And hunger.
People used to phone like this when they didn't actually want to see each other.
Today you send each other texts instead. I don't call that progress, I call it laziness with a battery.
Vandalism of public property.
At last you're doing something I understand from the bottom of my heart. I'm almost a little proud of you.
Pizza without tuna is, if I may put it so plainly, nothing more than bread with an opinion.
A paper unicorn, and it's floating. I would catch it, but then my paws would be wet.
Wet paws for an animal that doesn't even taste of anything? I have principles, young man.
This is what rain sounds like when it's sad.
Which, by the way, is almost always. I've watched it for a long time, and it doesn't have good days.
She is absolutely right. Objects always know more than they admit.
Ask a vacuum cleaner what it's planning. It won't tell you, but it has a plan. It always has a plan.
Warm, and dry from below. I'm staying here.
Call me when the world is saved or when someone hands out tuna. I don't care which comes first.
It's raining. Still. I thought I'd mention it in case it escaped you.
It hasn't escaped me. Nothing that makes me wet ever escapes me.
The man in the hat is still staring at you. One of you has to blink eventually, and it won't be him.
The noodles are steaming, you're standing around, and I'm sitting.
So only one of the three of us is doing anything useful, and it isn't the noodles.
He doesn't check me, he nods at me, and I don't nod back.
That's my test, and he passes because he isn't offended. Very few manage that.
Four fingers per hand. I have four paws with five toes each. He's working it out. He's disappointed. We won't be friends.
A cardigan, soft and warm. I would sleep on it if he stood still.
He is standing still. Very still, in fact. I'm seriously considering it.
He's crying into his noodles and I'm sitting next to him. He stops for a moment. Then cries louder. I have that effect.
